captions.instagram:
How is buttermilk made?

Buttermilk has no butter in it. It is what the churn leaves behind once the butter is out, and it is also the name of a drink no churn ever touched. Churn a pot of dahi, watch the curd specks sink in a glass of chaas, pour a tadka, and work out why a cup of it makes a pancake rise.

→ Buttermilk is two drinks with one name: the liquid left after churning butter, and dahi beaten with water.
→ Churn dahi with cold water. Fat globules lose their skins, stick together and grow into grains of makhan.
→ Lift the makhan out. The water, protein, milk sugar and acid stay behind: that is traditional buttermilk.
→ Bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid. Near pH 4.6 the milk protein links up and the milk sets.
→ Churning breaks the gel into specks. They slowly sink, leaving clear whey on top. A stir fixes it.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/buttermilkclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How is buttermilk made? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Buttermilk has no butter in it. It is what the churn leaves behind once the butter is out, and it is also the name of a drink no churn ever touched. Churn a pot of dahi, watch the curd specks sink in a glass of chaas, pour a tadka, and work out why a cup of it makes a pancake rise.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/buttermilkclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/buttermilkclear

In this video:
• Two drinks, one name. Traditional buttermilk is the thin, sour liquid left when butter is churned out of dahi or soured cream.
• The churn takes the fat and leaves the rest. The mathani tears the skins off the fat globules, which stick into grains of makhan.
• Sour, thin, and it settles. Bacteria turn lactose into lactic acid and the pH falls from about 6.6 to 4.5.
• Water, salt and a tadka. The recipe is mostly one choice: how much water.
• The dairy and the oven. A dairy heats skim milk to about 90 °C, cools it to about 22 °C and sours it for 12 to 16 hours with Lactococcus and aroma-making Leuconostoc.
• It keeps souring. The bacteria are still alive, so chaas left out on a hot day turns sharply sour in hours, while a fridge almost stops them.
